propertyDefinitions.label: Tensile Strength
propertyDefinitions.description: Maximum uniaxial tensile stress a film or specimen can withstand before breaking or yielding under controlled strain.
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Depends strongly on film thickness, plasticizer content, crystallinity, conditioning relative humidity, and strain rate (e.g., ASTM D882 vs. ISO 527).

propertyDefinitions.label: Water Vapour Transmission Rate (WVTR)
propertyDefinitions.description: Steady-state rate of water vapour permeation through a unit area of film over 24 hours under a specified temperature and RH gradient.
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Cannot be compared directly across different thickness values, temperature settings (23°C vs. 38°C), or RH gradients (e.g., 50% RH vs. 90% RH under ASTM E96 / ASTM F1249).

propertyDefinitions.label: Water Contact Angle
propertyDefinitions.description: Static sessile-drop angle formed by distilled water on the polymer surface; indicates relative hydrophilicity (< 90°) or hydrophobicity (≥ 90°).
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Sensitive to surface roughness, plasticizer migration, casting solvent, and measurement equilibration time.

propertyDefinitions.label: Biodegradability
propertyDefinitions.description: Microbial assimilation and mineralization into CO2, H2O, and biomass under defined composting, soil, or marine conditions.
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Industrial composting (58°C, ISO 14855 / ASTM D6400) differs fundamentally from ambient soil or marine degradation (Emadian et al., 2017).

propertyDefinitions.label: Optical Transparency
propertyDefinitions.description: Fraction of visible light transmitted through the film (often measured at 550–600 nm or broadband per ASTM D1003), determining product visibility.
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Strongly influenced by polymer crystallinity, film thickness, drying kinetics, and presence of fillers or blends.

propertyDefinitions.label: Leaching / Migration
propertyDefinitions.description: Mass transfer of monomers, oligomers, plasticizers, or cross-linkers from packaging into food simulants under defined time-temperature contact.
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Evaluated against food-simulant protocols (aqueous, acidic, or fatty simulants such as EU 10/2011 or FDA 21 CFR); values depend on simulant and contact time.

propertyDefinitions.label: Humidity Response
propertyDefinitions.description: Sensitivity of mechanical stiffness, tensile strength, dimensional stability, or barrier rates to rising ambient relative humidity.
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Polysaccharide films (starch, cellulose, chitosan, alginate) exhibit moisture plasticization at high RH, whereas aliphatic polyesters (PLA, PHA) are comparatively less moisture-sensitive.

propertyDefinitions.label: Load-Bearing Capacity
propertyDefinitions.description: Maximum vertical, puncture, or burst load supported by a defined film specimen, pouch seal, or thermoformed tray before failure.
propertyDefinitions.comparabilityNote: Highly dependent on container geometry, wall thickness, and fixture design; standardized data for lab-cast thin films are often unavailable.

materials.name: PLA (Polylactic Acid)
materials.biobasedOrigin: Fermented plant sugars (corn starch, sugarcane, cassava)
materials.shortIntro: A rigid, optically clear aliphatic polyester synthesized from fermented plant dextrose, widely used in thermoformed trays, cups, and biaxially oriented films.
materials.introduction: Polylactic acid (PLA) is a thermoplastic aliphatic polyester derived from renewable carbohydrate feedstocks. It is one of the most commercially established bioplastics for rigid and semi-rigid food packaging due to its high modulus, gloss, optical clarity, and processability on conventional extrusion and thermoforming equipment.

chemicalStructure.formulaNote: Polymer of lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) existing in L-, D-, or racemic D,L-isomeric configurations; L-content governs crystallinity and thermal behaviour.

materials.sourceAndProduction: Starch or sucrose from maize, sugarcane, or tapioca is enzymatically hydrolyzed to glucose and fermented by Lactobacillus strains to lactic acid. Ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of cyclic lactide dimer yields high-molecular-weight PLA.
characteristics: High tensile modulus (~2.7–3.5 GPa) and glassy rigidity at room temperature (Tg ≈ 55–65°C).
High optical clarity and surface gloss comparable to PET or polystyrene in amorphous grades.
Moderate oxygen barrier, though water vapour permeability is higher than polyolefins (PE/PP).
Requires elevated temperature (~58°C) and microbial humidity for rapid biodegradation; degrades very slowly in ambient soil or marine water.
applications: Cold beverage cups and lids
Rigid thermoformed punnets for fresh berries, tomatoes, and salads
Bakery clamshells and dry confectionery window films
Biaxially oriented PLA (BOPLA) snack wrappers
advantages: Commercially scalable with established resin grades (e.g., extrusion, injection, film).
High transparency and printability for retail food presentation.
Lower greenhouse gas footprint in cradle-to-resin assessments compared with several petrochemical polymers.
limitations: Low heat deflection temperature (unmodified amorphous PLA softens near 55–60°C), limiting hot-fill or microwave use.
Brittle failure behaviour with low elongation at break (< 10%) unless toughened or copolymerized.
Does not biodegrade rapidly in home compost bins, landfills, or marine environments.
references: Marano, S., Laudadio, E., Minnelli, C., & Stipa, P. (2022). Tailoring the Barrier Properties of PLA: A State-of-the-Art Review for Food Packaging Applications. Polymers, 14(8), 1626.
Shi, X., Cui, L., Xu, C., & Wu, S. (2025). Next-Generation Bioplastics for Food Packaging: Sustainable Materials and Applications. Materials, 18(12), 2919.

Cruz, R. M. S., et al. (2022). Bioplastics for Food Packaging: Environmental Impact, Trends and Regulatory Aspects. Foods, 11(19), 3087.
Siracusa, V., Rocculi, P., Romani, S., & Dalla Rosa, M. (2008). Biodegradable Polymers for Food Packaging: A Review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 19, 634–643.
Peelman, N., Ragaert, P., De Meulenaer, B., Adons, D., Peeters, R., Cardon, L., et al. (2013). Application of Bioplastics for Food Packaging. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 32(2), 128–141.
Emadian, S. M., Onay, T. T., & Demirel, B. (2017). Biodegradation of Bioplastics in Natural Environments. Waste Management, 59, 526–536.

tensileStrength.testMethod: ASTM D882 / ISO 527 (literature film & molded range)
tensileStrength.formulation: Unmodified semicrystalline/amorphous PLLA commercial extrusion grades
tensileStrength.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); Peelman et al. (2013)
tensileStrength.notes: Orientation (BOPLA) increases tensile strength up to ~100 MPa along the draw direction; plasticization lowers tensile strength.

wvtr.testMethod: ASTM E96 / ASTM F1249 (standardized 25 µm film basis)
wvtr.reference: Peelman et al. (2013); Marano et al. (2022)
wvtr.notes: Higher WVTR than LDPE (~10–20 g/m²/day at 25 µm) or PET; barrier coatings (SiOx, AlOx) or multilayer structures are often studied for dry foods.

contactAngle.reference: Literature surface characterization studies (Siracusa et al., 2008 context)
contactAngle.notes: Moderately hydrophilic/wettable compared to polyolefins (~95–105°), yet far more water-resistant than native polysaccharides.

biodegradability.notes: In ambient soil (20–30°C) or marine water, degradation is substantially slower (< 15% over 100+ days) because Tg (~58°C) is not exceeded.

transparency.formulation: Amorphous or biaxially oriented PLA film
transparency.notes: Annealed high-crystallinity heat-resistant PLA grades turn opaque white due to spherulitic light scattering.

leachingMigration.value: Overall migration typically < 10 mg/dm² limit in tested aqueous/acidic simulants
leachingMigration.testMethod: EU Regulation No 10/2011 food-simulant immersion (e.g., 3% acetic acid, 10% ethanol)
leachingMigration.notes: Specific migration of lactic acid/lactide monomers increases in 50–95% ethanol or at temperatures above Tg (≥ 60°C); additive-dependent.

humidityResponse.value: Minimal tensile drop (< 10% variation between 20% and 85% RH at 23°C)
humidityResponse.testMethod: Conditioned tensile & WVTR testing across RH steps
humidityResponse.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); Peelman et al. (2013)
humidityResponse.notes: Low equilibrium moisture uptake (< 1 wt% at 50% RH) preserves dimensional rigidity better than starch or cellulose films, though hydrolytic cleavage accelerates in warm humid storage.

loadBearingCapacity.testMethod: No single standardized container load value across studies
loadBearingCapacity.sampleThickness: Varies by thermoformed wall thickness (200–600 µm)
loadBearingCapacity.notes: Top-load crush resistance depends on tray rib geometry and wall gauge; specific commercial container specifications must be tested per ASTM D2659 / ASTM D642.

materials.name: PHA / PHB (Polyhydroxyalkanoates)
materials.biobasedOrigin: Bacterial intracellular fermentation of plant oils, sugars, or VFAs
materials.biodegradationEnvironment: Industrial compost, soil, freshwater, and marine environments
materials.shortIntro: Intracellular microbial polyesters synthesized by bacteria as carbon-energy reserves, offering broader natural biodegradation including soil and marine media.
materials.introduction: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs)—including homopolymer poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) and copolymer poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV)—are linear polyesters produced directly inside microorganisms. Unlike PLA, PHAs are inherently biodegradable across a wide range of aerobic and anaerobic natural ecosystems.

chemicalStructure.formulaNote: Microbial aliphatic hydroxyalkanoate family where side-chain alkyl group R varies (methyl in PHB, ethyl in PHV), tuning crystallinity and flexibility.

materials.sourceAndProduction: Bacteria such as Cupriavidus necator or recombinant E. coli accumulate PHA granules (up to 70–80% cell dry weight) under nutrient-limited fermentation of glucose, vegetable oils, or agro-industrial waste streams, followed by solvent or enzymatic cell lysis recovery.
characteristics: PHB homopolymer is highly crystalline and stiff, whereas copolymers (PHBV, PHBHHx) offer improved ductility and lower melting temperatures.
Superior water vapour barrier compared to unmodified PLA and hydrophilic polysaccharides.
Biodegrades in ambient soil, home compost, freshwater, and marine water without requiring thermophilic 58°C conditions.
Narrow thermal processing window near melting point (Tm ≈ 170–180°C for PHB) requires careful stabilization.
applications: Moisture-sensitive dry food pouches and laminated paperboard coatings
Injection-molded cutlery, caps, and rigid food containers
Dairy and fatty-food barrier films (when copolymerized as PHBV/PHBHHx)
Marine-degradable agricultural and seafood packaging
advantages: True multi-environment biodegradability (compost, soil, aquatic) confirmed across microbial ecosystems.
Better hydrophobic moisture barrier than starch, cellulose, or unmodified PLA.
High crystallinity and heat resistance (Tm up to ~175°C in PHB) relative to amorphous PLA.
limitations: Significantly higher production cost than PLA and petrochemical plastics due to fermentation and downstream extraction.
PHB homopolymer undergoes secondary crystallization during storage, causing progressive brittleness.
Lower optical transparency than amorphous PLA due to high spherulite crystallinity.
references: Shi, X., Cui, L., Xu, C., & Wu, S. (2025). Next-Generation Bioplastics for Food Packaging: Sustainable Materials and Applications. Materials, 18(12), 2919.
Şomoghi, R., Mihai, S., & Oancea, F. (2025). An Overview of Bio-Based Polymers with Potential for Food Packaging Applications. Polymers, 17(17), 2335.
Rosenow, P., Fernández-Ayuso, C., López-García, P., & Minguez-Enkovaara, L. F. (2025). Design, New Materials, and Production Challenges of Bioplastics-Based Food Packaging. Materials, 18(3), 673.
Perera, K. Y., Jaiswal, A. K., & Jaiswal, S. (2023). Biopolymer-Based Sustainable Food Packaging Materials: Challenges, Solutions, and Applications. Foods, 12(12), 2422.
Siracusa, V., Rocculi, P., Romani, S., & Dalla Rosa, M. (2008). Biodegradable Polymers for Food Packaging: A Review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 19, 634–643.
Peelman, N., Ragaert, P., De Meulenaer, B., Adons, D., Peeters, R., Cardon, L., et al. (2013). Application of Bioplastics for Food Packaging. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 32(2), 128–141.
Emadian, S. M., Onay, T. T., & Demirel, B. (2017). Biodegradation of Bioplastics in Natural Environments. Waste Management, 59, 526–536.

tensileStrength.formulation: Neat PHB and PHBV (5–12 mol% HV)
tensileStrength.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); Peelman et al. (2013)
tensileStrength.notes: Increasing 3-hydroxyvalerate (HV) comonomer lowers tensile strength slightly while substantially improving elongation at break.

wvtr.formulation: Compression-molded or extruded PHB / PHBV film
wvtr.notes: Among bio-based biodegradable polyesters, PHB/PHBV exhibits markedly lower WVTR than PLA and polysaccharides, approaching polypropylene-like moisture protection in thicker gauges.

contactAngle.notes: Higher surface hydrophobicity than starch, chitosan, or alginate films; exact angle varies with surface crystallization roughness.

biodegradability.value: 70–95% in compost (30–90 d); 30–80% in soil/marine (60–180 d)
biodegradability.notes: Extracellular PHA depolymerases produced by diverse soil and marine microbes enable degradation without industrial thermophilic conditions.

transparency.notes: High degree of crystallinity scatters visible light, yielding translucent milky films unless formulated as ultra-thin coatings or medium-chain-length PHA blends.

leachingMigration.value: Overall migration reported < 10 mg/dm² in aqueous & fatty simulants for purified grades
leachingMigration.notes: Downstream purification efficiency is critical to ensure negligible residual bacterial endotoxins, solvents, or processing nucleators.

humidityResponse.value: Low sensitivity; tensile properties remain stable across 30–80% RH
humidityResponse.notes: Hydrophobic polyester backbone resists water uptake (< 0.5 wt%), preventing severe RH-induced softening seen in polysaccharide films.

loadBearingCapacity.testMethod: Not standardized across general PHB/PHBV literature
loadBearingCapacity.notes: Secondary aging embrittlement in unblended PHB reduces impact load resistance over storage time; container-level testing is required.

materials.name: Starch-based Bioplastics
materials.biobasedOrigin: Maize, potato, cassava (tapioca), wheat, or rice starch
materials.biodegradationEnvironment: Home compost, industrial compost, and soil
materials.shortIntro: Abundant, low-cost polysaccharide films and thermoplastic starch (TPS) blends plasticized with glycerol or sorbitol for short-shelf-life dry and carry packaging.
materials.introduction: Native starch consists of linear amylose and branched amylopectin granules. Because native starch degrades before melting, it is gelatinized and melt-processed with plasticizers (such as glycerol, sorbitol, or water) under shear and heat to form Thermoplastic Starch (TPS), often blended with PBAT or PLA for commercial packaging.

chemicalStructure.formulaNote: Polysaccharide composed of linear α-(1→4)-D-glucan (amylose) and branched α-(1→4)/α-(1→6)-D-glucan (amylopectin) chains.

materials.sourceAndProduction: Extracted from corn, potato, cassava, or wheat crops via wet milling, followed by extrusion or solution casting with 15–35 wt% polyol plasticizers (glycerol/sorbitol) and optional biodegradable polyesters (e.g., PBAT) to suppress retrogradation.
characteristics: Highly hydrophilic due to abundant hydroxyl (-OH) groups along the glucose backbone.
Low oxygen permeability under dry conditions (< 50% RH), making it attractive for dry oxidation-sensitive products if protected from moisture.
Prone to retrogradation (recrystallization and embrittlement over time) and rapid property loss at high humidity.
Readily degraded by ubiquitous amylolytic enzymes in soil and compost.
applications: Dry bakery bags, bread overwraps, and low-moisture snack liners (when blended with hydrophobic polyesters)
Expanded starch foam loose-fill cushioning and dry food trays
Soluble single-serve dry condiment or seasoning sachets
Carrier bags and produce sacks (typically TPS/PBAT blends)
advantages: Abundant agricultural feedstock availability and low raw polymer cost.
Rapid biodegradation in soil and home composting environments.
Good oxygen barrier at low relative humidity.
limitations: Very poor water vapour barrier (high WVTR) and susceptibility to swelling or dissolution upon direct liquid water contact.
Low mechanical tensile strength in unblended TPS films compared to PLA or synthetic plastics.
Severe plasticization and loss of stiffness above 65–75% RH.
references: Onyeaka, H., Obileke, K., Makaka, G., & Nwokolo, N. (2022). Current Research and Applications of Starch-Based Biodegradable Films for Food Packaging. Polymers, 14(6), 1126.
Perera, K. Y., Jaiswal, A. K., & Jaiswal, S. (2023). Biopolymer-Based Sustainable Food Packaging Materials: Challenges, Solutions, and Applications. Foods, 12(12), 2422.
Şomoghi, R., Mihai, S., & Oancea, F. (2025). An Overview of Bio-Based Polymers with Potential for Food Packaging Applications. Polymers, 17(17), 2335.
Siracusa, V., Rocculi, P., Romani, S., & Dalla Rosa, M. (2008). Biodegradable Polymers for Food Packaging: A Review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 19, 634–643.
Peelman, N., Ragaert, P., De Meulenaer, B., Adons, D., Peeters, R., Cardon, L., et al. (2013). Application of Bioplastics for Food Packaging. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 32(2), 128–141.
Emadian, S. M., Onay, T. T., & Demirel, B. (2017). Biodegradation of Bioplastics in Natural Environments. Waste Management, 59, 526–536.

tensileStrength.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); Peelman et al. (2013)
tensileStrength.notes: Higher glycerol content reduces tensile strength sharply while raising elongation; amylose-rich starches yield stronger films.

wvtr.reference: Peelman et al. (2013); Onyeaka et al. (2022)
wvtr.notes: Values span a wide range because moisture diffusivity increases exponentially with ambient RH and plasticizer fraction; blending with PBAT or wax coatings reduces WVTR.

contactAngle.notes: Strongly hydrophilic surface (< 60°); water droplets rapidly spread and absorb into uncrosslinked starch films.

biodegradability.notes: Native starch component degrades rapidly via microbial α-amylases; blend co-polymers (e.g., PBAT or PCL) dictate final mineralization rate.

transparency.notes: Extruded TPS/PBAT commercial bags are typically translucent to opaque white rather than optically clear.

leachingMigration.value: High glycerol & soluble carbohydrate leaching in aqueous media; requires hydrophobic barrier for wet food
leachingMigration.notes: Unmodified TPS swells and loses plasticizer in contact with high-moisture foods; therefore restricted mainly to dry foods unless laminated.

humidityResponse.value: Severe moisture uptake (> 15–30 wt% at ≥ 75% RH); sharp tensile strength drop & swelling
humidityResponse.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); Peelman et al. (2013)
humidityResponse.notes: Water acts as a potent secondary plasticizer, lowering tensile modulus and exponentially increasing gas/vapour permeability above 65% RH.

loadBearingCapacity.value: Data not available (unblended TPS unsuitable for wet structural loads)
loadBearingCapacity.testMethod: Not standardized for neat TPS films
loadBearingCapacity.notes: Commercial TPS/PBAT carry bags are rated via dart-drop or bag-drop tests (e.g., IS/ISO standards), which vary by blend ratio and thickness.

materials.name: Cellulose-based Materials
materials.biobasedOrigin: Wood pulp, cotton linters, agricultural residues (bagasse, bamboo)
materials.biodegradationEnvironment: Regenerated cellulose degrades in soil/compost; highly substituted cellulose acetate degrades slowly
materials.shortIntro: Versatile plant-derived polymers spanning regenerated cellulose films (cellophane) and esterified derivatives (cellulose acetate) with high tensile strength and optical gloss.
materials.introduction: Cellulose is the most abundant natural polymer on Earth. For packaging films, it is processed either as regenerated cellulose (via viscose or NMMO/Lyocell dissolution—known commercially as cellophane) or chemically esterified into thermoplastic cellulose derivatives such as cellulose acetate (CA) or nanocellulose barrier coatings.

chemicalStructure.formulaNote: Linear β-(1→4) glucan chain forming dense intra- and intermolecular hydrogen-bond networks; derivatives substitute C2, C3, C6 hydroxyls (e.g., acetyl groups in CA).

materials.sourceAndProduction: Dissolving wood pulp or cotton linters are purified and regenerated into thin films via xanthate/viscose or NMMO dissolution, or acetylated with acetic anhydride to produce melt-processable cellulose acetate; coated grades use nitrocellulose or PVDC/bio-wax moisture barriers.
characteristics: High mechanical tensile strength and stiffness due to extensive hydrogen bonding and high crystallinity.
Regenerated cellulose films provide excellent clarity, dead-fold properties, and low dry-state oxygen permeability.
Uncoated cellophane is moisture-sensitive; commercial food packaging grades typically apply thin moisture-barrier coatings.
Degree of substitution (DS) strongly controls biodegradability—unmodified cellophane degrades rapidly, whereas high-DS cellulose acetate degrades slowly.
applications: Twist-wrap confectionery and baked goods (high dead-fold retention)
Dry tea, coffee, spices, and pasta pouches (barrier-coated regenerated cellulose)
Transparent window cartons for bakery and fresh produce
Nanocellulose oxygen-barrier inner coatings on paperboard
advantages: High tensile strength and dimensional stiffness at thin gauges (20–35 µm).
High optical transparency and grease/oil resistance in dry environments.
Non-melting thermal stability up to ~180–200°C (regenerated cellulose).
limitations: Uncoated regenerated cellulose has very high WVTR and swells in humid conditions.
Regenerated cellulose cannot be heat-sealed directly without a heat-sealable coating layer.
Viscose chemical processing raises environmental effluent concerns unless closed-loop solvent systems are used; high-DS derivatives lose rapid biodegradability.
references: Şomoghi, R., Mihai, S., & Oancea, F. (2025). An Overview of Bio-Based Polymers with Potential for Food Packaging Applications. Polymers, 17(17), 2335.
Perera, K. Y., Jaiswal, A. K., & Jaiswal, S. (2023). Biopolymer-Based Sustainable Food Packaging Materials: Challenges, Solutions, and Applications. Foods, 12(12), 2422.
Cruz, R. M. S., et al. (2022). Bioplastics for Food Packaging: Environmental Impact, Trends and Regulatory Aspects. Foods, 11(19), 3087.
Siracusa, V., Rocculi, P., Romani, S., & Dalla Rosa, M. (2008). Biodegradable Polymers for Food Packaging: A Review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 19, 634–643.
Peelman, N., Ragaert, P., De Meulenaer, B., Adons, D., Peeters, R., Cardon, L., et al. (2013). Application of Bioplastics for Food Packaging. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 32(2), 128–141.

tensileStrength.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); Peelman et al. (2013)
tensileStrength.notes: Machine-direction (MD) strength in regenerated cellulose often exceeds 100 MPa; transverse direction (TD) is lower due to sheet orientation.

wvtr.formulation: Uncoated regenerated cellulose vs. coated commercial cellophane
wvtr.notes: Must distinguish uncoated hydrophilic cellulose (high WVTR) from commercial barrier-coated cellulose films engineered for moisture protection.

contactAngle.notes: Abundant free hydroxyl groups make uncoated regenerated cellulose strongly wettable; esterification raises contact angle.

biodegradability.value: Regenerated cellulose: > 80% in compost/soil (30–90 d); Cellulose acetate: slow, DS-dependent
biodegradability.formulation: Uncoated regenerated cellulose vs. cellulose acetate (DS ~2.5)
biodegradability.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); Peelman et al. (2013)
biodegradability.notes: Synthetic coatings or high degree of acetyl substitution (> 2.2) significantly retard microbial cellulase accessibility.

transparency.notes: Comparable to oriented polypropylene and PET windows for bakery and dry-food visibility.

leachingMigration.value: Low polymer migration for pure cellulose; depends on plasticizer (e.g., glycerol/PEG) & lacquer coating
leachingMigration.testMethod: EU 10/2011 & regenerated cellulose film Directive 2007/42/EC context
leachingMigration.notes: Softeners (polyols) used in regenerated cellulose can migrate into wet foods unless separated by an inner food-contact lacquer.

humidityResponse.value: Substantial softening & O2 barrier loss above 70% RH in uncoated films; coated grades remain stable
humidityResponse.notes: Oxygen transmission rate can jump by an order of magnitude as RH exceeds 75% in uncoated cellulose due to hydrogen-bond disruption.

loadBearingCapacity.value: Data not available (film-only material; requires rigid substrate for load)
loadBearingCapacity.testMethod: Not applicable as standalone rigid load-bearing container
loadBearingCapacity.notes: Used primarily as flexible wrapping/lidding or laminated onto molded pulp/paperboard trays for structural load.

materials.name: Chitosan-based Films
materials.biobasedOrigin: Deacetylation of chitin from crustacean shells (shrimp/crab waste) or fungal cell walls
materials.biodegradationEnvironment: Soil, compost, and enzymatic biological media
materials.shortIntro: Cationic aminopolysaccharide films valued in active food packaging research for intrinsic antimicrobial activity, film-forming ability, and grease resistance.
materials.introduction: Chitosan is a linear cationic copolymer obtained by alkaline deacetylation of chitin, the second most abundant natural biopolymer after cellulose. Soluble in dilute organic acids (e.g., 1% acetic or lactic acid), chitosan casts into cohesive, semi-transparent films with notable antimicrobial and oxygen-barrier properties at low humidity.

chemicalStructure.formulaNote: Random copolymer whose properties depend on Degree of Deacetylation (DD, typically 70–95%) and molecular weight (Mw).

materials.sourceAndProduction: Chitin recovered from seafood processing by-products (shrimp/crab shells) or fungal biomass undergoes demineralization, deproteinization, and concentrated NaOH deacetylation. Films are predominantly produced by laboratory solution casting from dilute acidic aqueous solutions.
characteristics: Polycationic amino groups (-NH3+ below pKa ~6.3) impart broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against food spoilage bacteria and fungi.
Good oxygen barrier and grease resistance under dry conditions.
Currently produced mostly via solution casting rather than melt extrusion, as chitosan decomposes prior to melting.
Mechanical and barrier behaviour varies strongly with acid solvent type, glycerol plasticizer, and DD.
applications: Edible antimicrobial coatings on fresh fruits, berries, and minimally processed produce
Active food packaging interleavers or surface coatings for chilled meat and poultry
Antioxidant/antimicrobial active nanocomposite films (research stage)
Specialty thin wraps for short-term perishable preservation
advantages: Valorizes seafood/crustacean waste streams into functional biopolymers.
Intrinsic antimicrobial and film-forming properties without synthetic biocides.
Biodegradable and non-toxic in tested food-coating research contexts.
limitations: Not melt-processable (thermally degrades before melting), limiting high-speed industrial film extrusion.
High water vapour permeability and swelling in wet or acidic environments unless crosslinked or blended.
Slight amber/yellowish tint and potential acetic acid odour if residual solvent is not neutralized/removed; allergen disclosure considerations for crustacean-derived grades.
references: Perera, K. Y., Jaiswal, A. K., & Jaiswal, S. (2023). Biopolymer-Based Sustainable Food Packaging Materials: Challenges, Solutions, and Applications. Foods, 12(12), 2422.
Shi, X., Cui, L., Xu, C., & Wu, S. (2025). Next-Generation Bioplastics for Food Packaging: Sustainable Materials and Applications. Materials, 18(12), 2919.
Şomoghi, R., Mihai, S., & Oancea, F. (2025). An Overview of Bio-Based Polymers with Potential for Food Packaging Applications. Polymers, 17(17), 2335.
Siracusa, V., Rocculi, P., Romani, S., & Dalla Rosa, M. (2008). Biodegradable Polymers for Food Packaging: A Review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 19, 634–643.
Peelman, N., Ragaert, P., De Meulenaer, B., Adons, D., Peeters, R., Cardon, L., et al. (2013). Application of Bioplastics for Food Packaging. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 32(2), 128–141.

tensileStrength.formulation: Medium-Mw chitosan (DD 75–90%) cast from 1% v/v acetic acid
tensileStrength.reference: Siracusa et al. (2008); published chitosan film characterization studies
tensileStrength.notes: Values vary considerably by molecular weight, acid counterion (acetic vs. lactic), and glycerol plasticizer concentration.

wvtr.reference: Published active-film literature (Peelman et al., 2013 context)
wvtr.notes: Note lower test temperature (25°C) compared to standard 38°C/90% RH polyester tests; direct numerical comparison with PLA/PHA at 38°C is invalid without normalization.

contactAngle.notes: Despite moderate initial contact angles due to acetylated segments, prolonged water contact causes film swelling.

biodegradability.value: Rapid enzymatic & soil degradation (> 70% mass loss reported in 30–60 days in active soil)
biodegradability.testMethod: Soil burial & lysozyme/chitinase enzymatic assays (non-standardized lab protocols)
biodegradability.notes: Formal ISO 14855 industrial certification datasets are less common for standalone cast chitosan than for commercial resins like PLA/PHA.

transparency.value: 70–88% at 600 nm (slight amber/yellow tint at UV-blue wavelengths)
transparency.notes: Lower transmittance in 280–400 nm UV range can offer partial UV-light protection for lipid-rich foods.

leachingMigration.value: Swelling and partial dissolution in acidic aqueous food simulants (pH < 5.5); data test-specific
leachingMigration.notes: Protonation of amine groups in acidic foods triggers swelling or release of incorporated active compounds; neutralization or crosslinking reduces leaching.

humidityResponse.value: Marked water sorption above 65% RH; tensile strength decreases while elongation rises
humidityResponse.notes: At elevated RH (> 75%), oxygen barrier drops significantly due to plasticization of the hydrogen-bonded network.

loadBearingCapacity.value: Data not available (not established for load-bearing packaging)
loadBearingCapacity.testMethod: No standardized structural load-bearing test data
loadBearingCapacity.notes: Chitosan is studied as a thin functional coating, edible wrap, or composite layer rather than a standalone load-bearing container.

materials.name: Alginate-based Films
materials.biobasedOrigin: Extracted from brown seaweeds (Phaeophyceae, e.g., Laminaria, Macrocystis)
materials.biodegradationEnvironment: Soil, compost, and aqueous microbial media
materials.shortIntro: Water-soluble seaweed polysaccharide films capable of ionic crosslinking with divalent calcium ions (Ca2+) to form cohesive, transparent edible coatings and sachets.
materials.introduction: Alginates are anionic linear polysaccharides harvested from brown marine macroalgae. Sodium alginate dissolves readily in water to cast clear films, while immersion or treatment with divalent cations (especially Ca2+) creates an ionic 'egg-box' crosslinked network that improves water resistance and mechanical cohesion.

chemicalStructure.formulaNote: Linear anionic copolymer of M- and G-uronic acid residues; guluronate (G) blocks selectively chelate Ca2+ ions to form crosslinked hydrogel networks.

materials.sourceAndProduction: Brown seaweed biomass is washed, acid-treated, and alkali-extracted to yield soluble sodium alginate. Packaging films are produced via aqueous solution casting (often with glycerol) followed optionally by CaCl2 bath crosslinking.
characteristics: Forms transparent, glossy, oil-resistant films from purely aqueous solutions without organic solvents.
Ionic crosslinking with Ca2+ converts water-soluble sodium alginate into water-insoluble calcium alginate hydrogels.
Good oxygen and lipid barrier at low relative humidity.
Non-thermoplastic; decomposes on heating rather than melting.
applications: Edible water-soluble dry soup, coffee, and seasoning pouches
Calcium-crosslinked protective dip coatings for fresh-cut fruits and vegetables
Oil-resistant wrapping membranes for low-moisture bakery or cheese portions
Active antioxidant/antimicrobial carrier films (research stage)
advantages: Renewable marine feedstock requiring no arable land or freshwater irrigation.
Mild aqueous casting process and food-grade E-number regulatory familiarity (sodium/calcium alginate as food additives).
Tunable water insolubility via simple food-safe Ca2+ crosslinking.
limitations: Uncrosslinked sodium alginate dissolves rapidly on contact with liquid water.
High water vapour transmission rate (WVTR) even after calcium crosslinking.
Cannot be processed via standard plastic melt extrusion or injection molding.
references: Perera, K. Y., Jaiswal, A. K., & Jaiswal, S. (2023). Biopolymer-Based Sustainable Food Packaging Materials: Challenges, Solutions, and Applications. Foods, 12(12), 2422.
Şomoghi, R., Mihai, S., & Oancea, F. (2025). An Overview of Bio-Based Polymers with Potential for Food Packaging Applications. Polymers, 17(17), 2335.
Siracusa, V., Rocculi, P., Romani, S., & Dalla Rosa, M. (2008). Biodegradable Polymers for Food Packaging: A Review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 19, 634–643.
Peelman, N., Ragaert, P., De Meulenaer, B., Adons, D., Peeters, R., Cardon, L., et al. (2013). Application of Bioplastics for Food Packaging. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 32(2), 128–141.

tensileStrength.formulation: Sodium alginate + 20–30% glycerol vs. CaCl2-crosslinked film
tensileStrength.notes: G-block rich alginates crosslink more densely with Ca2+, achieving higher tensile strength and reduced elongation.

wvtr.notes: Measured mostly at 25°C; inherently hydrophilic uronate backbone offers minimal moisture vapour barrier without lipid or wax layering.

contactAngle.formulation: Cast alginate films before and after CaCl2 crosslinking
contactAngle.notes: Strongly hydrophilic surface; water droplets rapidly wet uncrosslinked sodium alginate films.

biodegradability.value: Rapid microbial/soil breakdown (weeks in moist compost/soil)
biodegradability.formulation: Unblended sodium or calcium alginate film
biodegradability.notes: Marine and soil bacteria produce alginate lyases that depolymerize the uronate chain; standardized ISO 14855 data for commercial sheets remain limited.

transparency.notes: Excessive CaCl2 surface precipitation or phase-separated lipid additives reduce optical transmittance.

leachingMigration.value: Uncrosslinked Na-alginate dissolves in water; Ca2+-crosslinked films may exchange Ca2+ / glycerol in aqueous media
leachingMigration.notes: Suitable as an intentionally edible/dissolvable dry sachet or as a Ca2+-crosslinked coating; chelators in food can soften Ca-alginate networks.

humidityResponse.value: High moisture sorption above 60% RH; film softens and loses tensile stiffness
humidityResponse.notes: Ca2+ crosslinking lowers equilibrium water swelling compared to Na-alginate, though high-RH tensile softening still occurs.

loadBearingCapacity.value: Data not available (thin edible/coatings film; non-structural)
loadBearingCapacity.testMethod: No standardized load-bearing packaging test data
loadBearingCapacity.notes: Alginate films are designed for thin pouches, casings, or coatings rather than rigid load-bearing containers.
